en: Let's continue with these important
principles, though as mentioned before, we
already covered the 2 most important ones
when it comes to writing clean code.
Nonetheless, let's next have a look at the
Interface Segregation Principle. What is
this principle about?
The Interface Segregation Principle says
that many client-specific interfaces
are better than one general-purpose
interface.
Now again, as always,
what does this mean?
I got another example for you. I got a class
SQL database which implements an interface
called database.
Interfaces are a common thing in
object-oriented programming, of course.
Interfaces are contracts which force classes
to implement certain behaviors. In this
case, we are forced to add a connect and
store data method if we implement this
interface.
And the SQL database does implement this
interface.
Now everything looks all right here. But now
let's say we don't just have the SQL
database,
but instead we also have this in-memory
database, which of course also is a
database, and therefore it also makes sense
that we implemented the database interface.
Hence, we are forced to add a connect and
store data method.
And now the problem is that it might make
sense to have a store data method because no
matter if we are storing data in an SQL
database or in memory, we want to be able to
store data at the end of the day.
But connect,
that does not necessarily make sense here.
An in-memory database, which uses the local
memory for storing data doesn't really need
to connect anywhere.
So in the end, we have the wrong interface
here.
And if that kind of reminds you of the
Liskov Substitution Principle we had a look
at in the last lecture,
that would actually not be a surprise
because here we had the problem with
modeling our data incorrectly and using the
wrong base class in the end.
Now with the Interface Segregation
Principle, we have the problem of having a
wrong interface which we force onto multiple
classes,
even if these classes are not using
inheritance at all.
The problem is that our database interface
is a general-purpose interface here. It
tries to cover too many use cases,
connecting and storing data to be precise.
And we should avoid general-purpose
interfaces when following the Interface
Segregation Principle. Instead, we should
have multiple smaller client-specific
interfaces.
For example, here we could have a database
interface if we want to keep that name,
but in addition, we could have an interface
which is called RemoteDatabase,
and the connect method, forcing classes to
have a connect method, would go into
RemoteDatabase.
Then the SQL database class could implement
Database and RemoteDatabase,
which in TypeScript is done like this,
simply by separating interfaces by a comma.
And the in-memory database only implements
the Database interface and not the
RemoteDatabase interface.
Hence, we can delete connect here. We're not
forced to implement it anymore and hence we
now have code which does follow the
Interface Segregation Principle.
Now, just as with the Liskov Substitution
Principle,
obviously the Interface Segregation
Principle is an important principle when it
comes to writing maintainable and extensible
code.
When it comes to writing clean code,
where it of course matters that humans can
read the code quite well and that it's easy
to understand,
this rule doesn't help us too much.
It also doesn't hurt and it certainly helps
a bit, but it's not super important.
